newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - U.S. refiners to face another tough year.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - U.S. refiners to face another tough year.

text.p: Stiff competition, overcapacity and a growing flood of oil products are likely to drown any hopes for big profits at U.S. refineries next year, oil industry sources said.
"It's going to be a better year, but the reality is that refinery margins are definitely going to be under pressure," said Fadel Gheit, analyst at Fahnestock and Co in New York.
Margins have not been helped by the highest crude prices in over six years, which has raised costs for many independent refiners who cannot pass on much of that extra burden.
Gheit said any gains shown in refinery margins are likely to be short-lived and insignificant. "The bottom line is the tremendous oversupply of refining capacity," Gheit said.

Refiners saw few bright spots in 1996, with overall U.S. margins hovering near $3.78 a barrel for much of the year, according to Paul Ting, analyst with Salomon Brothers. The average break-even point for U.S. refineries is between $2.75 and $3.00, Ting said.
Not surprisingly, "Refiney Row" on the U.S. Gulf Coast was hardest hit in 1996 by the overcapacity, with margins breaking above $3.00 only during the fourth quarter, according to Ting.
East Coast margins also recovered in the fourth quarter, holding at $4.16 through mid-December, after averaging $2.98 for the third quarter and $3.88 in the second quarter.

Midcontinent refiners recorded a better year, peaking at $5.35 in the second quarter before sliding to $4.06 in the third quarter and $4.57 so far in the fourth, while California margins peaked at $9.05 in the second quarter but declined steadily to fourth quarter levels at $4.43.
There is little relief in sight, said John Lichtblau, chairman of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation in New York, unless refiners start shutting down excess capacity.
"You would think an industry operating at 94 or 95 percent (of capacity) would seem to be doing well," Lichtblau added.
Paulo Nery, analyst with Pace Consultants in Houston, is projecting U.S. margins to average about $3.80 a barrel in 1997, a touch better than the 1996 average.
"I see crude prices coming down, though gasoline will stay a little strong," Nery said.

Much of the U.S. refining industry is geared to process light crude oil, said Ken Miller, senior principal with the Houston consultancy Purvin & Gertz Inc. That means refiner margins hinge largely on gasoline prices.

"Margins can't ride on distillates," Miller said, referring to heating oil, diesel and jet fuel, which make up about 20 percent of the crude barrel. Gasoline on the other hand, makes up at least 50 percent of the crude barrel.
But Miller expected the market volatility to decline in the coming year, which could moderate the cost-conscious, just-in-time inventory mentality that has gripped the oil industry in the last year.
Sources note keeping lower stocks has created a sense of shortages, which is one reason crude prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange this year nearly touched $27 a barrel.

But the high prices are concentrated on barrels for prompt delivery, which has created a price structure referred to in financial markets as backwardation. For refiners, this has meant cutting stocks, raising output -- and more volatility.

But some said backwardation may ease in 1997 based on a slide in crude prices from current levels of about $25.00 a barrel, on output increases in the North Sea, South America and the return of limited amounts of Iraqi oil.
Still, few sources were optimistic that a drop in crude oil prices will boost refining margins in the coming year.

"There has been a complete de-coupling of crude costs and refinery margins," said Fahnestock's Gheit referring to the cut-throat competition that has made oil products markets' march to beat of their own drum.
Refiners will meanwhile continue to cut costs, either by modernizing operations or by forming alliances with other refiners or marketers in order to survive the competition.
"There've been tremendous efficiency gains in the refining industry," said William O'Keefe, executive vice-president of the American Petroleum Institute, an oil industry trade group.
"But because the gasoline market is so competitive, a lot of the gains have gone to the consumers," O'Keefe said.

One saving grace for margins should be continued U.S. demand growth for crude oil and refined products, even though projected growth of one to 1.5 percent in 1997 will be well off growth seen in 1996 rate of 2.5 percent.

But market analysts noted one big unknown is how much crude refiners in developing nations will push up crude prices as global competition for refinery feedstocks heats up. "Upward price pressure is going to come from the Far East, which is going to attract barrels that would otherwise go to the U.S," according to Pace's Nery, echoing other analyst comments that much of the surging petroleum demand in the world today is coming from Asia.
